title: Chickenomical's visual direction
question: Which visual world should guide the nearby chicken comparison screen?

options.label: The Guest Check
options.lineage: Diner guest checks and carbon-copy arithmetic
options.thesis: Every nearby offer reconciles into one clear check: count, total, unit price, source, and time.
options.viewport: A standard mobile app shell leads with current location, nugget or tender selection, and the lowest price per piece; a running tally resolves the cheapest requested quantity below the offers.
options.risk: Literal receipt styling can feel nostalgic and cramped; use no texture or faux paper controls.

raised.raise: Keep the quantity solver distinct from filter-reset actions.

raised.from: The Video Feed's Complete First Result
raised.raise: Show one fully sourced offer before any scroll or gesture.
Use tabular figures so prices and totals align at a glance.
Keep source and check time attached to the exact offer they qualify.

options.label: The Weekly Circular
options.lineage: Neighborhood grocery circulars and shelf-edge unit-price labels
options.thesis: Make the unit price the thing shoppers see first, then let them inspect the offer behind it.
options.viewport: A standard mobile results shell keeps location and category controls familiar; compact offer rows make the unit-price column dominant, with a single savings band on the current best offer.
options.risk: Sale graphics can imply an unverified discount; the highlight must mean lowest verified unit price only.

challengers.label: Decision Bands
challengers.thesis: Turn a local price comparison into one crisp next decision, with distance and freshness easy to scan.
challengers.viewport: Keep standard app navigation and controls; reserve a strong yellow band for the current best-value offer and use a restrained split-flap update when the ranking changes.
challengers.case: Competitive on product clarity: distance, status, and a next choice read quickly; weaker audience identification because airport wayfinding is not a food-value cue.
challengers.risk: Yellow can overpower price evidence or be mistaken for a warning if it fills the whole screen.

challengers.label: The Annotated Price Sheet
challengers.lineage: Reference-setting pages with a ruling rail and annotation margin
challengers.thesis: Keep each offer's price, count, source, and check time visibly connected.
challengers.viewport: Use a standard mobile result list; a thin red bracket ties each total to its source note, while controls and navigation stay platform-native.
challengers.case: Declined on audience identification and task fit: the publishing idiom asks shoppers to read an edition instead of scanning nearby offers.
challengers.kept: Keep provenance beside the offer it explains, even when the list becomes dense.
challengers.risk: A rail can become hard to read at phone widths; keep source notes inline with the offer.

challengers.label: The Ticket Wallet
challengers.lineage: Jet-age airline ticket wallets and carbon-copy coupons
challengers.thesis: Sequence a requested quantity from selected offers to one final total.
challengers.viewport: A quantity request becomes a sequence of coupon-like offer states.
challengers.case: Declined on both axes: itinerary language feels unrelated to local food shopping, and ticket metaphors suggest booking or checkout outside the MVP.
challengers.kept: Keep active, stale, and unavailable offer states explicit; state changes remain visible.
challengers.risk: A ticket-book sequence makes the comparison feel transactional.

challengers.label: The Console
challengers.thesis: A dense graphite surface separates work areas with hairline seams.
challengers.viewport: A panel grid places location, filters, and results in persistent work areas.
challengers.case: Declined on both axes: the console reads as a specialist workbench and hides a simple consumer comparison behind technical panels.
challengers.kept: Give the quantity action its own breathing space, separate from filter reset.
challengers.risk: A technical dashboard would make the product feel built for operators.

challengers.label: The Vertical Feed
challengers.thesis: One result fills the screen, then snaps to the next.
challengers.viewport: A single offer occupies each full-height page with a gesture-led move to another.
challengers.case: Declined on both axes: the audience needs to compare several exact offers together, and full-bleed media hides the evidence that makes a result useful.
challengers.kept: Show one complete, source-attributed offer before any scroll or extra gesture.
challengers.risk: A swipe-only result flow makes side-by-side comparison difficult.

challengers.label: The Type Specimen
challengers.thesis: One type axis changes every number and label as the user drags.
challengers.viewport: A weight slider morphs the offer list and its price figures together.
challengers.case: Declined on both axes: font manipulation is not a value-shopper task and animated prices threaten legibility.
challengers.kept: Use tabular figures so totals align without continuous animation.
challengers.risk: A moving type system could make factual prices harder to read.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A polished mobile comparison list with familiar filters, a clear price-per-piece sort, and source-linked offers.
canonCard.viewport: A standard location field, category control, unit-price ranking, complete offer rows, and a secondary quantity solver.
canonCard.risk: Familiar by design, with little visual distinction from other comparison apps.
